d.name: Malaria
d.why: Malaria can rapidly become severe and life-threatening if not diagnosed and treated promptly.
d.desc: Malaria is a life-threatening but preventable and curable infectious disease. It is caused by Plasmodium parasites and is transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito. The greatest burden of malaria occurs in sub-Saharan Africa, including Ethiopi
d.cause: Malaria is caused by five species of Plasmodium that infect humans. The two most important species are: > Plasmodium falciparum > Plasmodium vivax In Ethiopia, both species occur, but P. falciparum is responsible for many severe case
d.risk: People at higher risk of severe malaria include: > Children under 5 years > Pregnant women > People living with HIV/AIDS > Travelers without immunity > People living in malaria-endemic areas

d.name: Tuberculosis (TB)
d.why: Tuberculosis is a serious disease. If it is not diagnosed and treated early, it can damage the lungs and other organs, spread to other people, and may result in death. Drug-resistant TB is even more difficult to treat and requires specialized medical care
d.desc: Tuberculosis (TB) is a preventable and curable infectious disease caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It most commonly affects the lungs (pulmonary TB), but it can also affect other organs such as the kidneys, brain, spine, and lymph nodes. TB spreads through the air when a person with active pulmonary TB coughs, sneezes, speaks, or spits. Without early diagnosis and proper treatment, TB can become severe and may be fatal.
d.cause: Tuberculosis is caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Infection occurs when a person inhales tiny airborne droplets released by someone with active pulmonary TB. Although many infected people develop latent TB infection and do not become ill immediately, some progress to active disease, especially if their immune system becomes weakened
d.risk: People are at increased risk of developing active TB if they have one or more of the following ; > HIV infection > Diabetes mellitus > Undernutrition (malnutrition) > Smoking > Harmful alcohol use > Weak immune system > Close contact with a person who has active TB > Living in crowded or poorly ventilated environments

d.name: Pneumonia
d.why: Pneumonia can become life-threatening if it is not treated promptly. Severe pneumonia may cause respiratory failure, bloodstream infection (sepsis), or death, particularly in children, older adults, and individuals with weakened immune systems. Early medical evaluation and appropriate treatment are essential
d.desc: Pneumonia is an infectious disease that causes inflammation of the air sacs (alveoli) in one or both lungs. The air sacs may fill with fluid or pus, making breathing difficult and reducing the amount of oxygen that reaches the body. Pneumonia can be caused by bacteria, viruses, or fungi and ranges from mild to life-threatening, especially in young children, older adults, and people with weakened immune systems. Early diagnosis and appropriate treatment greatly improve recovery and reduce complications.
d.cause: Pneumonia is caused by microorganisms such as bacteria, viruses, and fungi that infect the lungs. Common bacterial causes include Streptococcus pneumoniae, while respiratory viruses such as influenza virus and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) are also frequent causes. Infection spreads mainly through respiratory droplets released when an infected person coughs or sneezes. The risk of illness increases when the body's immune defenses are weakened.
d.risk: People are more likely to develop pneumonia if they have one or more of the following risk factors: > Children younger than five years > Adults aged 65 years and older > Weak immune system > Chronic diseases (such as diabetes or heart disease) > Smoking > Indoor air pollution > Malnutrition > Exposure to infected individuals

d.name: Diarrheal Disease
d.why: Although many cases are mild, diarrheal disease can rapidly become life-threatening because of severe dehydration and electrolyte loss, especially in infants, young children, older adults, and people with weakened immune systems. Prompt treatment with oral rehydration solution (ORS), zinc supplementation (for children where appropriate), and medical care for severe cases can prevent complications and death.
d.desc: Diarrheal disease is a preventable and treatable infectious disease characterized by the passage of three or more loose or watery stools within 24 hours. It is usually a symptom of an infection affecting the intestinal tract and can be caused by bacteria, viruses, or parasites. If not treated promptly, especially in young children, it can lead to severe dehydration, malnutrition, and even death. Globally, diarrheal disease remains one of the leading causes of illness and death among children under five years of age.
d.cause: Diarrheal disease is commonly caused by infections from bacteria, viruses, or parasites. These microorganisms spread through contaminated food, unsafe drinking water, poor sanitation, and inadequate hygiene. Common bacterial causes include Escherichia coli, Salmonella, Shigella, and Campylobacter. Viral causes include rotavirus and norovirus, while parasites such as Giardia and Cryptosporidium can also cause infection.
d.risk: People are at greater risk of diarrheal disease if they have one or more of the following: > Drinking unsafe or contaminated water > Poor sanitation and hygiene > Lack of handwashing with soap > Eating contaminated or improperly prepared food > Malnutrition > Weakened immune system > Living in overcrowded environments > Children under five years of age

d.name: Intestinal Worm Infection (Helminthiasis)
d.why: Most intestinal worm infections are mild, but heavy or repeated infections can cause anemia, malnutrition, abdominal pain, intestinal blockage, poor physical growth, and impaired learning in children. Early diagnosis and treatment help prevent these complications.
d.desc: Intestinal worm infection, also known as soil-transmitted helminthiasis, is a parasitic disease caused by intestinal worms such as roundworms, whipworms, and hookworms. People become infected by swallowing parasite eggs from contaminated soil, food, or water, or through skin contact with contaminated soil in the case of hookworms. These infections are common in tropical and subtropical regions, including Ethiopia, especially where sanitation and access to clean water are limited. Heavy infections can affect nutrition, growth, learning, and overall health.
d.cause: Intestinal worm infections are caused by parasitic worms, mainly: > Ascaris lumbricoides (roundworm) > Trichuris trichiura (whipworm) > Hookworms (Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus) The parasites spread through contact with contaminated soil, poor sanitation, inadequate hygiene, and consumption of contaminated food or water.
d.risk: People are more likely to develop intestinal worm infections if they: > Have poor sanitation > Lack access to clean water > Do not wash hands properly > Walk barefoot on contaminated soil > Eat contaminated food > Live in tropical or subtropical regions > Are school-age children > Live in areas with poor hygiene infrastructure

Urgent need to have a bowel movement

p.name: Garlic
p.prep: Fresh bulb is crushed and taken orally, sometimes mixed with water or honey. Preparation varies among Ethiopian communities.
p.use: Traditionally used in Ethiopia to help manage malaria symptoms and other infectious illnesses. It is also widely used for intestinal worms, coughs, and general immune support in traditional medicine.
p.warn: Traditional medicinal use only. It should not replace WHO-recommended antimalarial medicines.
ref: WHO – Guidelines for the Treatment of Malaria

p.name: Bugleweed
p.prep: Fresh leaves are crushed or boiled to prepare a decoction.
p.use: Traditionally used for treating malaria and fever in several Ethiopian communities.
p.warn: Traditional use only; dosage and safety are not standardized.
ref: PubMed – Ethiopian antimalarial medicinal plant review

p.name: Broad-leaved Croton
p.prep: Leaves are boiled in water and the decoction is taken orally.
p.use: Traditionally used for malaria, fever, and other infectious illnesses.
p.warn: May cause adverse effects if used improperly; traditional use does not establish clinical efficacy.
ref: PubMed – Ethiopian antimalarial medicinal plant review

p.name: Papaya
p.prep: Leaves are crushed or boiled to prepare a traditional remedy.
p.use: Leaves are traditionally used in some Ethiopian communities for malaria and fever.
p.warn: Traditional use only; not recommended as a replacement for standard malaria treatment.

p.name: Garden Cress
p.prep: Seeds are ground into powder and mixed with water or food before oral administration.
p.use: Traditionally used to help manage malaria and febrile illnesses in Ethiopia.
p.warn: Traditional use only; scientific evidence remains limited.
ref: PubMed – Review of Ethiopian medicinal plants used against malaria

p.name: Garlic
p.prep: Crushed fresh bulb, sometimes mixed with honey or water
p.use: Traditionally used for tuberculosis, chronic cough, and chest infections
p.warn: Not a substitute for anti-TB drugs
ref: PubMed – Traditional medicinal plants used in the treatment of tuberculosis in Ethiopia

p.name: Ginger
p.prep: Fresh rhizome boiled as a decoction
p.use: Traditionally used for persistent cough, sore throat, and respiratory illness
p.warn: May interact with blood-thinning medicines; not a replacement for TB treatment
ref: Ethiopian Medicinal Plants Used for Respiratory Tract Disorders Review

p.name: Broad-leaved Croton
p.prep: Leaves or roots boiled to prepare a decoction
p.use: Traditionally used to manage tuberculosis and respiratory infections
p.warn: Excessive use may be toxic; professional guidance is recommended

p.name: African Boxwood
p.prep: Root decoction prepared with water
p.use: Traditionally used for tuberculosis and glandular swellings
p.warn: Safety in pregnancy and long-term use has not been established

p.name: Ethiopian Basil
p.prep: Fresh leaves boiled or crushed for infusion
p.use: Traditionally used to relieve cough, fever, and respiratory symptoms associated with chest illnesses
p.warn: Traditional remedy only; not a replacement for approved TB medicines
ref: Ethiopian Medicinal Plants Used for Respiratory Tract Disorders Review

p.name: Ethiopian Basil
p.prep: Fresh leaves are boiled to prepare an infusion or inhaled as steam.
p.use: Traditionally used for pneumonia, cough, fever, common cold, and respiratory infections.
p.warn: Not a substitute for antibiotics or hospital treatment for pneumonia.
ref: PubMed – Ethiopian Medicinal Plants Used for Respiratory Tract Disorders

p.name: Garlic
p.prep: Fresh bulb is crushed and taken with honey or water.
p.use: Traditionally used for pneumonia, chronic cough, and chest infections.
p.warn: May interact with blood-thinning medicines; not a replacement for antibiotics.
ref: PubMed – Review of Ethiopian respiratory medicinal plants

p.name: Ginger
p.prep: Rhizome is boiled to prepare a decoction.
p.use: Traditionally used to relieve cough, sore throat, chest congestion, and pneumonia symptoms.
p.warn: High doses may cause stomach irritation; not a replacement for medical treatment.

p.name: Rue
p.prep: Leaves are crushed or boiled to prepare an infusion.
p.use: Traditionally used for cough, pneumonia, influenza, and chest pain.
p.warn: May be toxic in large doses and should be avoided during pregnancy.
ref: PubMed – Ethiopian medicinal plants for respiratory diseases

p.name: Eucalyptus
p.prep: Leaves are boiled and the steam is inhaled or prepared as an infusion.
p.use: Traditionally used to relieve cough, breathing difficulty, pneumonia, and other respiratory infections.
p.warn: Essential oil should not be swallowed undiluted; not a replacement for antibiotics.
ref: PubMed – Ethiopian Medicinal Plants Used for Respiratory Tract Disorders

p.name: Coffee
p.prep: Roasted seeds prepared as coffee; some communities use preparations traditionally for stomach problems and diarrhea.
p.use: Traditionally used for gastrointestinal disorders including diarrhea in some Ethiopian communities.
p.warn: Excessive caffeine intake may cause stomach irritation; not a replacement for ORS or medical treatment.
ref: Systematic review of Ethiopian medicinal plants

p.name: Garden Cress
p.prep: Seeds crushed into powder and taken with water or food.
p.use: Traditionally used for diarrhea, stomachache, and digestive problems.
p.warn: High amounts may cause digestive irritation.

p.name: Ethiopian Cardamom
p.prep: Seeds crushed and used traditionally in preparations.
p.use: Traditionally used for stomach disorders, diarrhea, and digestive complaints.
p.warn: Excessive use may cause gastrointestinal discomfort.

p.name: African Wormwood
p.prep: Leaves prepared as infusion or decoction.
p.use: Traditionally used for digestive complaints and infectious illnesses.
p.warn: Avoid excessive use; safety and dosage are not standardized.

p.name: Guava
p.prep: Leaves boiled in water to prepare a decoction.
p.use: Traditionally used for diarrhea and dysentery.
p.warn: Severe diarrhea requires ORS and medical evaluation.
ref: International ethnopharmacology literature on Psidium guajava

p.name: Garlic
p.prep: Fresh bulb is crushed and mixed with water or honey.
p.use: Traditionally used to expel intestinal worms and manage digestive complaints.
p.warn: Large amounts may cause stomach irritation; not a replacement for prescribed anthelmintic medicines.

p.name: Garden Cress
p.prep: Seeds are ground into powder and mixed with water or food.
p.use: Traditionally used for intestinal worms and stomach disorders.
p.warn: Use in moderation; excessive intake may irritate the stomach.

p.name: Ethiopian Wormwood
p.prep: Leaves are boiled to prepare a decoction.
p.use: Traditionally used against intestinal worms and gastrointestinal ailments.
p.warn: Avoid excessive use; safety during pregnancy has not been established.

p.name: African Boxwood
p.prep: Root is boiled to prepare a decoction.
p.use: Traditionally used to manage intestinal worms and abdominal pain.
p.warn: Safety has not been well studied; avoid self-medication for severe illness.

p.name: Ethiopian Basil
p.prep: Fresh leaves are boiled to prepare an infusion.
p.use: Traditionally used for stomach disorders, intestinal worms, and digestive discomfort.
p.warn: Traditional remedy only; seek medical care for persistent worm infections.
